Building a white, cable-hidden RTX 5080 with Claude

An admittedly silly quest to find an all-white 5080 that could go "stealth". A PNY donor card, a laser-cut powder-coated backplate, a bent-metal cable cover and 94 versions of cut files later, here's how it went, including everything that didn't work.

Graf3X, October 2026 · Code, cut files and templates on GitHub

Phase 1 · July

"It's how much?!"

Every quest needs a damsel in distress and a villain. In this story, the damsel is me, and the villain is VRAM.

My fabulous wife is a talented Fallout 4 builder and her creations had grown into sprawling, ambitious masterpieces. Her 10 GB video card was buckling under the weight. After hours of tinkering we found VRAM lurking behind every stutter and crash. She simply didn't have enough of it.

Unfortunately, I knew the solution: she needed a 5070 Ti. Just like the one in my machine.

One quick swap later, her machine was running flawlessly, and I had a brand-new problem to solve.

Now, of note: I had a black PNY 5070 Ti in my all-white PC build, a build with rear connectors for everything except the power for the video card. Great chance to correct both of those and maybe get a little upgrade.

Or so I thought.

I sent Claude out to do some "deep research" for me. What is out there, what is white, what is near white, what has hidden connectors, why is stealth not just the BTF standard? All the fun stuff.

  1. RTX 5080 or better.
  2. White, or at least not all black. This one relaxed over time.
  3. A hidden or relocated power connector. The one rule that never bent.

After a ton of back and forth, we found listings in China with hidden power connectors for the 40 series, and a 5090 "stealth" card, but no 80 series. Weird.

CandidateWhy it looked goodWhy it failed
ASUS TUF RTX 5080 BTFNo visible cable at allIts GC-HPWR gold finger needs an ASUS BTF board. Stealth boards have no such socket.
Colorful iGame Ultra ZConnector hidden under a magnetic backplate panelThe RTX 50 line dropped that design. It tops out at 5070 Ti
Gigabyte Stealth IceGigabyte's own hidden-connector designOnly shipped on the 5090
AX Gaming X3W MaxWhite, recessed connector, custom L-cableChina only. No retail listing anywhere
AORUS 5080 Infinity WoodHidden connector, works on any boardReal, but not sold in the US at first

What's that? A light at the end of the tunnel?

The Gigabyte AORUS RTX 5080 Infinity Wood. Hidden connector and it works on any board. Hey Claude, how much do you think it will cost?

Claude figured over $2,000. It was working from the $5,300 price of the 5090 version. For reference the RTX 5080's MSRP is $999.

"Good luck finding one anywhere near that this summer. The cheapest one I found was $1,289.99." -Claude

What.

Well, that might be worth it, but let's see what it would cost to make my own versus something that isn't even available.

Wait and watch. Claude started to say it thought it might be a limited run, only in certain regions, or a paper launch. Still, it ticked all the boxes, so let's wait it out. I had Claude set up a scheduled task to check stock and price twice a day. It kept running even with my PC asleep.

Then it showed up in France at TopAchat for €1,999.99. Claude found it in stock on the AORUS EU store for €1,632.12. But that store only ships to six EU countries. None of them mine.

Back in January Taiwan's card makers had already raised RTX 50 prices 10–15% because of the memory shortage. Cards with 16 GB or more (like mine) went up 15–20%.

Once I challenged Claude on the $2,000 price, it became less confident. The 5090 sits on NVIDIA's own exotic board and the 5080 sits on a normal Gigabyte one. On July 31st the Infinity Wood was on Newegg US for $1,899.99. That made it the high water mark, anything close to that I should just get the Infinity.

Phase 2 · early August

From buying to building

So with that decided, what could I make? I have been on YouTube long enough to hear about SendCutSend's fabrication services, maybe I can use them? (With a backup of JLC3DP)

My first idea was a white shroud boxing in the whole card. But then I would have to worry about the fan headers and fan location, so I avoided that (for now). It would also hide the WireView Pro II I was thinking about buying.

OK then. What about a cable channel? Just a metal box down to the board's pass-through. It reinforces the cable's bend radius.

The first version was an L. It ran straight down the card from the connector and turned once along the bottom edge. That got changed into a double bend later when I realized the power connector would not clear the RAM.

Phase 3 · August 8–9

Picking a donor

This is where I moved from chatting with Claude to Claude Code. It wrote everything into a gpu-mod folder on my PC and put together a full build brief.

The big pick was the donor card. A PNY RTX 5080 OC Triple Fan at $1,289.99 was the cheapest new 5080 anywhere at the time. But price wasn't the whole story. What mattered was how each card behaves once you take it apart.

CardPriceVerdict
PNY OC Triple Fan$1,289.99Picked. Cheapest, and a clean donor.
Zotac Solid Core OC$1,299.99Backplate is an active cooling part
ASUS Prime$1,354.93Best-documented deshroud, proprietary 7-pin fan header
PNY ARGB Epic-X OC$1,399.99Same PG147 board. $110 more for 45 MHz and RGB I'd throw away
Gigabyte Gaming OC$1,499.99Thermal putty, unrestorable after teardown

No one has published a teardown of this card, or measurements. So an Alphacool waterblock manual for the board family and a PNY 5070 Ti modder's post became my guide until I had the card in hand.

The backplate as a constraint map

The vents radiate out from the GPU die. Near the die they stay small. The thermal pads there need solid metal so the plate can work as a heatsink. Over the bare fin stack they get big because airflow there is free. My logo Graf3X is cut right through the field. It brands the plate and it moves air.

Every part comes out of Python from one config file. That file had a flag in it called MEASURED.VERIFIED = False, so every script announced that its geometry was still a guess.

Before spending a cent on metal the backplate went through SendCutSend's online quoter to give me a quick early estimate. $68.26 cut and powder coated in RAL 9003 gloss white.

Phase 4 · mid August

5000 series and the 12V-2x6 burnt plugs

Before I even started down this path I was thinking about getting a WireView Pro II for my 5070 Ti. A coworker of mine had his video card very recently get crispy, and I had seen all of the news coverage about melting connectors, so it just seemed sensible. After the plan of running the power down the side of the card came up, using a WireView as a 180° adapter with a fancy screen just lined up nicely, get my 180 turn, get the added protection, two birds one WireView Pro II.

Till the card arrived.

I don't think that's going to work.

For the curious: on this card the connector sits at the bottom of a well 26.61 mm deep. The plug-in WireView's plug only reaches about 13 mm below its body. It comes up 13.6 mm short.

So that throws the whole plan into jeopardy. A quick email to Thermal Grizzly confirms that yes, it will not fit on that card. And no, they have no plans to sell a white version of the WireView Pro II Wired edition anytime soon.

OK, so we'll revisit that one later. First, let's focus on the backplate.

Phase 5 · late August

Measure twice, cut once. Then measure again.

Every single hole that held a screw on the designs was a guess. An educated guess from a waterblock manual and some other guy's 5070 Ti mod. Time to dig into getting real measurements for this 5080 card.

My iPhone's LiDAR? No. Claude let me know it was ±5–10 mm, not nearly enough precision for the screw holes.

So, the flatbed scanner. At 300 dpi every pixel is about 0.085 mm and that's plenty. One problem though. The plate is 326 mm long and my scanner is letter size. So it went through in overlapping passes, six of them for the outside face alone, turned every which way. The plan said to tape the rule to the plate, but the rule was shorter than the card, so that would not have helped here.

Then the calipers. I own two pairs, they are 13 years and 10 years old respectively. Do they agree? I measured a titanium Apple Card with both and got 85.59 and 85.55 mm. Obviously the Neiko is the one that's off, right?

Claude: not so fast. The card made out of a precious metal (titanium) is still ±0.12 mm. With no known reference two calipers can only agree or disagree. Nobody's wrong yet.

No reference, no verdict.

Two PEC Tools metal rulers and two gauge blocks (one 100 mm and one 4 inch) became the real reference. Every critical number comes off the same instruments so whatever it's off by cancels out.

The paper prototype

I wanted to have a physical way to cheaply verify our prototypes would work. I originally wanted it for the cable channel only but it became invaluable doing the backplate:

  • The 180° adapter hit the edge of the stock notch by about 3.45 mm. So the notch got wider (4 mm, then 3 more as a cushion).
  • The plate prints as two tiles that overlap by 12 mm. The first caption said to butt them edge to edge. Do that and you get a 336 mm plate for a 324 mm card. The tiles now have a seam line and DO NOT BUTT printed right on them.
  • The fold marks didn't say which way to fold. Fold a skin the wrong way and you get its mirror image. They now say 45 UP and 45 DOWN.
  • The skin sheets had a solid cut line drawn across the root of every tab. Cut them out as printed and all nine tabs fall right off.

Amazon Basics printer paper is $6.97 for 500 sheets. That's about 1.4 cents a sheet and the backplate template took two. Metal is $68 and a week of shipping.

Phase 6 · August 20–23

Thirteen holes

Most numbers on this plate could be a millimeter off and nobody would ever notice. The screw holes can't. Claude was adamant that it would prefer to find the holes through code, and that my squishy jelly hands and eyes would give inaccurate measurements. So I let it churn on this. Four days, three detectors and six corrections that went nowhere. In the end it took me with an image editor drawing circles by hand to get it exactly correct.

Click here to skip to what worked ↓

The plan: scan it and let the computer find the holes

So off came the stock backplate and onto the scanner it went. 31 scans at 300 dpi. Claude calibrated the scanner first from a scan of my PEC Tools rulers by themselves on the glass. An inch is exactly 25.4 mm by definition so that works great. The scanner came out within 0.08% on both axes. Six scans of the die window in four different orientations agreed on its area to 0.07%. So far so good. That part was solid and it stayed solid.

Then came the holes.

Claude wrote a detector to go find them. Version one looked for a bright ring around a dark center. It found the QR sticker. Great. Version two looked for a bright hole inside a dark countersink and found pretty much nothing. Turns out the scanner lamp lights each countersink from one side so the hole itself comes out black.

Third time's the charm. Claude cut a few real holes out of one scan and had the detector hunt every other scan for that exact lopsided glint. The lamp always comes from the same side so every hole looks the same. It found 7 to 13 holes per scan.

Well, "worked." Then I noticed it was calling the letters in the PNY logo screw holes. Claude added a size filter. Then one hole got counted twice. Then one "hole" turned out to be the corner of a decorative cut-out that no automatic test could reject. That one got excluded by hand because I said so.

Stitching, or where "a few off" came from

No single scan saw the whole plate, so the passes had to be stitched together, and the only thing to line them up on was the holes themselves.

The passes disagreed with each other by 0.30 mm on average and 0.66 mm at worst. Stitch all of that together and you get 25 holes on a plate that has 13.

Claude came up with three theories. Maybe one scan pass was bad. Maybe the scanner glass was distorting things. Maybe the plate wasn't sitting square. It tested all three and all three were wrong. The evidence for the third one turned out to be a bug itself.

Learning: run the one-command test first

Claude's own log from that night pretty much admits it. It argued each idea before it measured anything. Two of the three tests used a setting it picked to get the answer it expected. The one test that settled anything was a single command. It could have run that one first.

Paper, and six corrections that went nowhere

So back to paper. Claude laid the pattern out 1:1 across two sheets. A hole seen in two or more scans got a solid ring. A hole seen in only one got a dashed ring. Each sheet also had a 100 mm bar on it marked MEASURE THIS FIRST. Good thing too. My printer drew it at 93.89 mm because "fit to page" had quietly shrunk everything by 6%. Thanks printer.

Most of those dashed rings turned out to be made up. 11 of the 25 holes were ghosts left over from all the rotating and rescanning. The next print dropped them.

To find where the real holes were I did a pencil rubbing. Tape the print to the card and rub a pencil over the paper. Each real hole shows up as a gray smudge next to its printed circle. Every hole sat on the same side of its circle about half a millimeter off. Same direction everywhere? That looks like the whole pattern is just shifted. Easy. One number to fix. So Claude shifted it.

Over Aug 22 it shifted the pattern five times and it never settled. Then we reset and it shifted a sixth time.

#Read againstWhat happenedRunning total (mm)
1Printed text on the sheet0.5 mm one way. One early reading had already come back mirrored.−0.50, +0.50
2Printed textHelped, didn't center. Another 0.5 mm the same way.−1.00, +1.00
3A compass rose added to the sheet1.25 mm south and east. That nearly cancelled 1 and 2+0.25, −0.25
4CompassCame out flipped on both axes. So the correction got reversed−2.25, +2.25
5Card partsPut a hole 0.34 mm from the plate edge. Everything zeroed.−2.75, +1.50
6Card parts, on a fresh print1.5 mm on each axis, identical at both far-end holes−1.50, +1.50

Part of the problem was just words. I'd read an offset off the paper as "right and down." Claude then had to translate that from the sheet to the plate to the side of the plate facing the card. Somewhere in there it flipped. So Claude added a compass rose to the sheet. The next reading came back flipped on both axes anyway.

What finally worked was naming directions after parts of the card. "Toward the DisplayPort end." "Toward the PCIe edge." Turn the paper over all you want and those don't flip.

The bigger problem was that shifting was the wrong fix to begin with. One print had the fin stack end lining up and the DisplayPort end off almost everywhere. So the error changed along the length of the plate. No single offset is ever going to fix that.

Learning: a two-point fit fixes two points

At one point Claude proposed stretching the pattern to match the two far end holes I'd measured with calipers. It matched those two holes perfectly. It also pushed the edge of another hole 1.09 mm off the plate. Yeah, we didn't use that one.

Fewer scans, then my eyes

At this point I just wanted it done, and I wanted to be sure the holes were on the correct spots, not nearly, but exactly the correct spot.

So Claude built me a review page instead. Every candidate showed up as a little crop zoomed in 4×. I rejected the ones that weren't holes. Then I opened each real hole in Paint, made a circle selection, copy-pasted it and lined up the selection so I could not see the bottom-right edge anymore. Read the numbers off of the scan, gave them to Claude.

And there it was. The detector itself was biased. It put each center on the darkest pixels in the hole and the darkest pixels are the shadowed top edge. So every single detection got dragged about 1.7 mm off. I'd also noticed the plate has two styles of hole. Some are recessed and some have a collar. Once we sorted them by style the rest of the bias showed up clean.

Here's the kicker. Claude had suggested exactly this early on, but didn't raise it up, it gleefully kept trying to solve the problem. It ran a test that didn't settle anything and then dismissed the idea on a check that turned out to be wrong. Its note in the code is blunt. The paper corrections had been fighting a detector bias with a placement constant.

Oh and one more trap. The review page numbered the holes column by column. Later a script rebuilt the list and sorted it row by row. So every hole number was quietly wrong. That snuck a 1 mm error into the plate's width before a column check caught it.

The pattern that got cut

The final pattern came straight from my measurements. 11 holes from one scan and 5 from the other with 3 seen in both. 11 + 5 − 3 = 13. That's the same count I got by hand on the actual plate. Then we checked it against things that had nothing to do with building it:

CheckResult
The 3 holes seen in both scansAgree to 0.02, 0.27 and 0.34 mm
Columns across the plate0.12, 0.13 and 0.18 mm of scatter. The last column was at 1.81 mm until one bad reading was redone.
Plate length implied by the holes326.30 mm against a rule reading of 326.3 ± 1.5
1:1 print on the cardAt the far end the printed hole falls inside the stock hole

We also stopped chasing precision the part didn't actually need. The screw only has to clear the hole. So the clearance holes went from 2.55 to 3.2 mm. That gives 0.6 mm of play. Nylon washers give the screw heads something to sit on. Three holes were too close to the PCIe edge to leave the 2 mm of metal SendCutSend needs. They couldn't move. So they became slots that open to the edge.

The photo at the top of this page is the first test fit. Every screw went right in.

Learning: the person holding the part is the best sensor

The code was great at counting and measuring. But every fix that mattered came from me actually looking at the plate. The logo letters, the decorative cut-out, the two hole styles and the 13 hole count were all things I spotted. The pattern only settled once my eyes were the input and the code did the checking. Not bad for squishy jelly hands.

Phase 7 · August 24–25

94 vent designs and a logo a computer could read

With the holes finally nailed down I could see where the vents could go. The PCB stops 180 mm from the bracket end. Past that it's nothing but fin stack behind the plate. No pads, no components and nothing to keep clear of. Between 210 and 313 mm there aren't any screw holes at all either. That's where the card exhausts its air. PNY's own chevron vent sits there too and it opens 39.1 cm².

Then I made one call that changed everything. Claude had been holding every vent design to "no worse than stock airflow." That was Claude's own instinct. I never asked for it. My case has five intake fans blowing up and over the card so airflow was never going to be this card's problem. That made open area purely a looks thing. In exchange I asked for one thing. Give me the open area number on every design, every time, without me having to ask.

Over six rounds that turned into 94 designs. The biggest surprise was that busy doesn't mean open. It's the shape you build the pattern out of that decides it:

PatternLooksOpen
ghost-x, 76 openingsIntricate11%
trace, 24 openingsComplex27%
shear, 49 openingsSimple44%
stealth, facetedComplex47%

I shortlisted eight and Claude spotted what they all had in common. None of them were really "composed." Each one is a single rule repeated across the whole plate. So the plate reads like the output of a function. Which meant I couldn't just slap the Graf3X logo on like a sticker. It had to be part of what the rule draws.

Making the OCR read it

Can you read the logo? That stopped being my opinion. Claude ran every version through an OCR with 62 templates covering upper case, lower case and digits. Each letter had to beat all 61 wrong answers to count.

Most of them failed. A pattern like this only puts about four rows across a capital letter and a letter needs about eight to read. What passed was cutting the letters inside a quiet zone where the pattern stops. Three designs made it through: Interference, Interference long wave and Bit Plane.

Then the font came back to bite us. On Aug 30 an audit found the "a" holding a little island of metal on a 0.99 mm neck. That's half of SendCutSend's 2 mm minimum. Thicker strokes open up the cut but they thin out the metal around it. No weight of Arial Bold could do both. So Claude ran a sweep of fonts and sizes:

Face and widthNarrowest cutThinnest metalOCR
Arial Bold 82 mm1.7502.007Reads, cut too narrow
Arial Bold 96 mm1.8922.218Reads "3raf3X"
Bahnschrift 82 mm2.0502.170X too weak
Bahnschrift 90 mm2.0942.400Reads Graf3X on all three

Funny thing is Bahnschrift was the font the config was supposed to be using all along. Somewhere along the way it got switched to Arial Bold and nothing noticed.

The vents also kept running into the cover. In the first production files 15 of the 19 cover parts clashed with a vent. Later audits pulled the vents out from under the cover's glue and out of the channel floor where the cable lies. I put that last one back at release. Now the pattern runs across the whole plate including under the channel. That way if the cover ever comes off the plate still looks right. The same pattern even runs through the cover's roof.

Phase 8 · August 25–28

Six cable covers in four days

The backplate we could measure. The cable cover had to come from nothing. It went through six layouts before one stuck. Almost every time the thing that killed a design only showed up once we drew it a different way. Whether that was 3D, flat 2D, a solid model, a flat pattern or folded up out of card stock.

WhenDesignWhat killed it
Aug 25One bent hat-section following the routeA wall can't follow the top around a corner without being cut. That meant eight relief cuts and four of them on the side facing my logo.
Aug 25Five straight pieces joined with "dovetail" fingersDrawing the joint flat found four bugs the 3D view had hidden. A dovetail between two flat sheets overlaps itself so it can't exist. Then the tapered fix cancelled itself out. I asked if the slack in the spacing was real. It was 1.67 mm against the 0.70 it was supposed to be.
Aug 25Parallel fingers, checked as solidsIt worked. Zero overlap and every joint could go together. Then I changed the rules. The side facing my logo had to be one perfect bent and painted surface with no seams and no cuts.
Aug 26Split along the run. Then parts that meet at the cornersCloser. But they left 28 mm openings where the cable turns and seams at both corners.
Aug 26Ribbon and plate. A flat top with no bends and walls made of strips that only fold around vertical linesZero relief cuts. SendCutSend says a bend across a part's full width doesn't need any. But on the 45° route a 40 mm mounting cleat needs 53.9 mm of straight wall and no leg was that long.
Aug 26–28Carcass and skins. A folded inner channel carries every relief cut and plain skins on the outside hide itBuilt. All the remaining work went into making it cuttable.

The turning point was my call. The one-piece design needed relief cuts at every corner and four of them landed on the side facing my logo. Nope. So I changed the rules. That side has to be one perfect bent and painted surface with no seams and no cuts.

When the corners still wouldn't cooperate Claude sent out seventeen research agents to look at the problem the way eight unrelated trades would. Six of the eight came back with the same answer. Separate the top from the walls. So that's what got built. A folded inner channel we called the carcass carries every relief cut where you can't see it. Plain outer skins hide it.

Learning: the 90° number is not the 45° number

Bend deduction is how much shorter the flat blank is than the folded part, and it changes with the angle. Claude had been using the 90° number of 2.95 mm on every fold. At 45° it's only 0.97 mm. Every blank would have come out about 4 mm short at every corner.

Small numbers that weren't small

  • The shadow line is the tape. That little gap you see between the skin and the carcass is the tape. So it had to be a thickness 3M actually makes. The 3.0 mm tape scored better on paper but it only comes in white. A white line in a groove on gloss white just looks like a smear. The gray 2.30 mm VHB 4991 looks like a shadow. Color won.
  • The adapter. I checked on the stock card and the backplate blocks the 180° adapter on the bracket side. That's the side we'd already widened the notch toward. So Claude took back a fix it had suggested the day before.
  • The cable. On Aug 28 I finally measured the cable itself. 22.0 × 6.0 mm. It fits everywhere. The top of the connector sits 14.29 mm above the PCB. That leaves 0.61 mm to spare under the cover's roof. Tight but it fits.
  • The carcass had never been unfolded. The first real flat pattern overlapped itself by 266 mm². We had drawn it, rendered it, priced it and printed templates of it. Nobody had asked if it could actually be cut.
Learning: draw it a different way

The 3D viewer hid four joint bugs that a flat drawing found. The flat drawing hid three more that only the math found. The flat pattern hid two feet that only collide once it's folded, and an audit only caught those by folding the part in software. Every new way of looking at it caught a new kind of mistake.

Phase 9 · August 29 – September 4

94 versions and a whole lot of checking

The cover got released on Sept 3 after 22 rounds of audits and the cut files hit v94 on Sept 4. 94 sounds crazy, I know. That's just what happens when every little change gets regenerated from code and checked again automatically.

GateWhat it checks
release_gate.pyAll 10 DXFs: the five parts and their upload copies
test_artefacts.pyPrinted PDFs: fold marks, tab counts, overprinting text
vent_ocr.pyThat each vent design still reads "Graf3X" by OCR
hardware.pyThe folded 3D model and the press brake, zero collisions

Not safe to cut

The first full audit ran on Aug 29. Twelve agents went through the files looking at them six different ways. Then a second agent was told to assume every finding was wrong and try to knock it down. The verdict still came back not safe to cut, 9 blockers. Here are a few of the catches. Any one of them would have meant scrapped metal.

WhenDefectWhat it would have done
Aug 29The carcass blank had no bend compensation at all4.2 mm too narrow and every fold in the wrong place
Aug 29Eight tapped holes placed in assembled coordinates on a flat patternEight holes down the middle of the cover's visible roof
Aug 30Fold direction appeared nowhere in the filesThe skins fold up, up, down, down. Fold them all one way and the show face is scrap.
Aug 31Both skins marked to fold into mirror images. Both fold checks agreedFour blanks scrapped. Coated 5052 cracks if you fold it back.
Aug 31Two feet that collide only once folded, by 9 mm² eachThe last bend wouldn't close on the press brake
Aug 31The bench instructions named the wrong tape for the feet2.30 mm tape lifts every tab 0.30 mm. No tab reaches its slot
Aug 31The notch capDidn't need it. It blocked the adapter. It needed 3.6 mm in a 2.4 mm gap. Dropped from the order.

For every fix Claude would plant the bug on purpose and make sure the check caught it. If a check has never failed how do you know it works? It also owned up to its own mistakes. In round two it overruled an auditor about a thin spot in the logo. The auditor was right. In round six it found out a fold check it had been quoting for three rounds had never actually run. The gate had been happily printing ALL CHECKS PASS the whole time. Claude's commit message said it best: A check that did not run is not a check that passed.

The last two measurements

By Aug 31 the whole cover came down to one question. Where exactly does the power connector sit in its notch? The channel had to clear a card screw on one side and the connector body on the other. If the connector sat dead center it would hit the cover's wall by 1.25 mm. No pressure.

Claude drew up how to measure it off the two closest card screws. One photo from me settled it. The connector sits at 148.32 mm and clears the wall by 2.47 mm even after powder coat. Then I put the calipers on the adapter and got 25.03 mm along the card. That clears with room to spare on every side. Nothing had to be cut.

Release, rejection and v94

Round 22 finished on Sept 1 with every check green. Then I saw the first full render and made four changes. I wanted an end cap at the plug end. I wanted the vents across the whole plate including under the channel, and I wanted the same pattern through the cover's roof. And I wanted "50/50" feet with tape on the show side and screws on the far side. I signed off on the new render and the cover was released on Sept 3.

SendCutSend's uploader rejected it the same day. It read the solid bend lines as cuts with zero width. Switching them to dashed lines fixed that.

Then I found the real last problem. SendCutSend won't powder coat a part narrower than an inch and the skins were 14.5 mm. Whoops. So I sketched a fix. Fold the bottom of each skin under into a foot, screw the feet to the backplate and stand the carcass on top of the feet. Claude checked it and built it and that became v94. SendCutSend can't countersink 2 mm stock either, so I countersink the screw holes by hand from the back after coating.

The box

The parts showed up bent, coated and looking perfect. They were also wrong. SendCutSend sent me the same skin side twice. Two of one side, none of the other and no way to build the cover.

After weeks of hunting down my own mistakes the one error that made it into the box was theirs. When I contacted them and told them what happened they escalated me immediately and started cutting me a free replacement. Can't fault that. And shout out to the SendCutSend CS team, seriously nice to talk to people who were empowered enough to solve the problem quickly and with very little back and forth.

My calls

I went with a hat-section carcass and flush skins. The 50/50 mount puts tape where you can see it and M2.5 screws where you can't so the cover stays removable. I only ordered one of the backplates. All of it is 2.0 mm 5052-H32 aluminum in RAL 9003 gloss white, cut and bent by SendCutSend. Every part clears their 1 inch powder coat minimum.

Matching the white

Powder coat only works on metal. That's a problem when the front of the card is vinyl and the WireView Pro II Wired only comes in black. So we looked up who makes SendCutSend's powder. It's Tiger Drylac. I ordered the matching white direct from them in spray can form and painted both.

How Claude was used

Quick reference. I worked with Claude three different ways on this and each one did a different job.

ToolWhat it did on this build
Claude chatMarket research, live price checks, arguing about designs, looking over photos of the card and figuring out how to measure it
Scheduled task (Cowork)Checked AORUS RTX 5080 Infinity Wood stock and price twice a day so I didn't have to
Claude CodeWrote all the CAD in Python, made the DXF cut files and 1:1 print PDFs, ran the design checks, priced out vendors and published the build pages

What didn't work and how we got around it

Almost all of this got caught on a screen or on paper before any metal got cut. Honestly that's the best argument for working this way.

What went wrongWorkaround
  • No card on the market met all three requirements
    Built one from a cheap black donor card
  • A full shroud would trap heat at the hottest connector
    Open cable channel instead
  • The plug-in WireView comes up 13.6 mm short in the recessed connector
    WireView Pro II Wired on a 40 cm pigtail
  • An early cable route bent ~30 mm from the connector. That's inside the 35 mm safe zone
    48 mm straight then two 45° chamfers. The build now fails under 35 mm
  • Impact left 7 too-thin metal webs in the logo. Then Arial Bold trapped an island on a 0.99 mm neck
    Bahnschrift at 90 mm. The one font and size that cuts clean and still reads Graf3X
  • Cleanup code was silently deleting shroud lettering
    An X monogram and a check that fails if a letter disappears
  • 3 × 120 mm fans need 360 mm on a 324 mm card
    Stock 3 × 100 mm fans or 2 × 140 mm with overhang
  • SendCutSend can't countersink 2 mm stock
    Low-profile heads on the card screws. I countersink the cover's screw holes by hand from the back
  • PCB assumed ~232 mm long
    It ends at about 180 mm. Vents regenerated
  • iPhone LiDAR is ±5–10 mm
    300 dpi flatbed scans calibrated off my PEC Tools rulers
  • "One caliper must be off"
    No reference, no verdict. Rulers and gauge blocks became the reference
  • The hole detector found a QR sticker. Then nothing. Then the PNY logo
    Matching the lamp's one-sided glint. Then filters for what I spotted by eye
  • Six stitched scans gave 25 "holes" on a 13-hole plate
    Dropped the single-scan ghosts. Then measured the centers by hand from two scans
  • Six paper corrections drifted and never settled
    The real error was a 1.7 mm detector bias. Measuring by hand found it
  • Directions flipped between paper and card. Even with a compass rose
    Name directions after card parts. DisplayPort end. PCIe edge
  • Hole numbers quietly got re-sorted by row instead of by column
    Positions now live with the data. A column check caught the 1 mm error
  • A ±0.3 mm hole target nobody questioned
    3.2 mm clearance holes with nylon washers
  • Vent patterns with the logo built in failed the OCR
    Letters cut inside a quiet zone. Checked against 62 templates
  • A one-piece bent cover needs eight relief cuts. Four land on the show side
    Carcass and skins. The cuts live on a hidden inner part
  • A "dovetail" joint between two flat sheets
    Can't exist. Parallel fingers, then no joint on the show side at all
  • The 90° bend deduction used at 45° folds
    Use the 45° number. Blanks were 3.97 mm short per corner
  • SendCutSend won't powder coat a part under 25.4 mm wide. The skin was 14.5 mm
    v94. The skins grow screwed-down feet and the carcass stands on them
  • Both skins marked to fold into mirror images
    A check that folds each blank the way the file says and lands its tabs in the slots
  • The tile caption said to butt the tiles. That makes a 336 mm plate
    Seam line and DO NOT BUTT printed right on the tiles
  • The adapter fouled the stock notch edge
    Found on a paper print. The notch got 4 mm wider, then 3 more
  • Claude claimed rebuilds were byte-identical
    Wrong. The DXF library stamps a timestamp. The geometry is identical though
  • The WireView Pro II Wired only comes in black
    Painted it and the card's front vinyl with Tiger Drylac white from a spray can
  • Some artifact viewers won't hand out .dxf files
    Save DXFs with a .txt suffix. Drop it before uploading
  • SendCutSend's uploader read solid bend lines as zero-width cuts
    Dashed bend lines. A 4 mm wall stub removed
  • SendCutSend shipped the same skin side twice
    They escalated me right away and cut a free replacement
Push back on Claude

It got numbers wrong. Every time I called one out it went back, checked and fixed it. If a number can scrap metal double check it.

Paper before metal

About three cents of printer paper caught problems that would have cost a $68 plate and a week of shipping.

Make the tests prove themselves

If a check has never failed you don't know it works. Plant the bug and watch it get caught.

Agree on which way is up

Six paper corrections failed because each one got read a different way. Name directions after parts of the card instead.

The person holding the part is the best sensor

The code counted and measured. Every fix that mattered on the holes came from me looking at the plate.

How it stacks up against the Infinity Wood

On paper the plan landed about even with the $1,899.99 Infinity Wood. But mine is white, hides its cable and keeps an eye on every pin of its own power connector. Nothing you can buy does all three. These numbers are from the Aug 8–9 build brief.

ItemPlanned (USD)
PNY RTX 5080 OC Triple Fan$1,289.99
WireView Pro II Wired$175.38
Backplates ×2, cut and coated$110.86
Planned total~$1,700–1,850
AORUS 5080 Infinity Wood, for reference$1,899.99

What did it actually cost? We don't talk about that.

Two lessons here. The metal is the cheap part. I only ordered one backplate, and a second one would have only been about $42 more. The cable channel parts came in around that much too. Next to a $1,289.99 card that's nothing. And put every white part on one order because powder coat batches drift.

The finished card

Going from "this card doesn't exist" to a one-of-one card took about seven weeks. Five chat sessions, a twice-daily scheduled task and more Claude Code sessions than I care to count. I set out on this project to create something with mostly AI and me guiding it along the way. I feel like it worked, and it worked well.

For those of you who are juggling a full time job, a part time job, a wife, kids, and playing video games I do suggest you grab your local AI and see how much it can help you get things done. I was pleasantly surprised by the result of this one. I do plan to do more to it, so stay tuned for more 🙂

Want to build one yourself or just poke around the code? Go check it out on GitHub at github.com/Graf3x/PNY5080-Custom-Backplate. The Python, the cut files and the paper templates are all in there.

Designed and built by Graf3X with Claude (chat, scheduled tasks and Claude Code). Parts cut and coated by SendCutSend.
